method_notes: Targeted closure of the Welsh non-sport gap in the UK major-event census (census previously held 65 Welsh venues, of which only 8 theatre/concert/auditorium and 1 conference/exhibition). Scope: Wales, >=1,000 capacity, NON-SPORT only. Existing census name+city pairs and alternative_names were extracted programmatically from venues.json before research began, and the four records here that re-use an existing canonical_name+city (Venue Cymru/Llandudno, Rhyl Pavilion Theatre/Rhyl, Royal Welsh Showground/Builth Wells, St David's Hall/Cardiff) are deliberate enrichments of records that previously carried capacity_value null and, in the case of St David's Hall, operational_status STATUS_REVIEW_REQUIRED. POPULATIONS CHECKED: all 22 Welsh council areas were worked through by name for non-sport venues of >=1,000 capacity; Business Events Wales / Meet in Wales (meetinwales.com) including its association-venue-capacity page and the North Wales regional pages; meetnorthwales.co.uk large-conference venue listing; Visit Wales / Visit Mid Wales / Show Me Wales destination directories; Denbighshire Leisure Ltd's event-venue estate; Wrexham University, Bangor University, Aberystwyth University, Swansea University and UWTSD Carmarthen commercial/venue estates; ATG (Swansea Arena, held), Academy Music Group (St David's Hall lease), Live Nation (new Cardiff Bay Arena) and Depot Live (Cardiff Castle, Blackweir) operator portfolios; the Royal Welsh Agricultural Society showground plus the Anglesey, Carmarthen (United Counties/Nantyci), Pembrokeshire (Withybush) and Denbigh & Flint showgrounds. DELIBERATE GEOGRAPHIC EMPHASIS: research started in North, Mid and West Wales rather than Cardiff. Of the 17 records here, 6 are North Wales (Wrexham, Llangollen, Rhyl x2, Llandudno, Anglesey), 2 Mid Wales (Aberystwyth, Builth Wells), 3 West Wales (Llanelli, Carmarthen, Haverfordwest) and 6 South-East Wales (Newport x2, Cardiff x4) - i.e. a majority outside the south-east. No geographic quota was imposed; this reflects what the evidence showed. ACCESS OBSTACLES AND ESCALATION: Business Events Wales /venues 404s and its search is client-rendered, so discovery went via councils, operator portfolios, universities and venues' own sites. Plain unauthenticated fetches (Level 1) were tried first throughout; aberystwythartscentre.co.uk and unitedcounties.org returned 403/blocked to a plain fetch and were then opened in a real browser (Level 3) to read the same public pages, which is how the Great Hall capacity and the Carmarthen Showground hire/what's-on facts were obtained. llanellitowncouncil.gov.uk returned a 403 'Security Check' to both a plain fetch and a browser session; that boundary was respected and not worked around, so the Selwyn Samuel Centre capacity is cited to a GRADE_B directory instead and its calendar is recorded as unestablished. cardiff.gov.uk, seetickets.com, showmewales.co.uk (partially) and celtic-manor PDF extraction were also unavailable; where that left a fact unproven it is recorded as unproven, not guessed. EXCLUSIONS - checked and rejected as genuinely sub-1,000, each with a cited figure: Theatr Clwyd, Mold - Anthony Hopkins Theatre 569 seats (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatr_Clwyd); Pontio, Bangor - Theatr Bryn Terfel 480 seats (pontio.co.uk/en/your-visit/the-centre); Princess Royal Theatre, Port Talbot - 798 (cvent venue page); Swansea University Great Hall, Bay Campus - 700-seat Sir Stanley Clarke Auditorium (conferencesandevents.swansea.ac.uk); Cardiff City Hall - Assembly Room 600 theatre-style, its largest room (cardiffcityhall.com/rooms/assembly-room/); The Vale Resort, Hensol - Castle Suite 700 theatre-style, its largest (valeresort.com/our-spaces/); Prichard-Jones Hall, Bangor University - 240 (bangor.ac.uk/weddings/venues); Halliwell Centre, Carmarthen (UWTSD) - theatre 325, main conference suite 200 (venuewales.co.uk); Grand Pavilion, Porthcawl - 643 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Pavilion,_Porthcawl); Y Stiwt, Rhosllanerchrugog - 490 seats (stiwt.com / Theatres Trust); Ffwrnes, Llanelli - 504 main auditorium (theatrausirgar.co.uk); Coal Exchange, Cardiff - Grand Hall Suite 800 reception / 400 theatre, its largest (coalexchangecardiff.co.uk/grand-hall-suite/). Also checked and left out for want of any evidenced >=1,000 event space or any capacity evidence at all: Pontins Prestatyn Sands (holiday park, closed with immediate effect 30 November 2023 - no capacity figure for its entertainment venue could be evidenced, so it is not recorded as a venue); Margam Country Park, Neath Port Talbot (hosts the In It Together festival and outdoor cinema but no capacity figure could be evidenced); Denbigh & Flint Show ground at The Green, Denbigh, Vale of Glamorgan Show at Fonmon and the Monmouthshire Show at Vauxhall Fields (annual one-day shows on fields rather than standing hireable showgrounds, and no first-party capacity); Singleton Park, Swansea. JUDGEMENT ON THE TRUE WELSH ESTATE: the previous pass's instinct was right - the genuine Welsh non-sport >=1,000 estate is small, and this pass has now evidenced why rather than assumed it. Outside Cardiff, Swansea and Newport, Wales has very few permanent indoor venues over 1,000: the North Wales estate above that line is essentially Venue Cymru, Rhyl Pavilion, Rhyl Events Arena, William Aston Hall and the Royal International Pavilion; Mid Wales is Aberystwyth Arts Centre and the Royal Welsh Showground; West Wales is the Selwyn Samuel Centre plus two county showgrounds. Every other significant Welsh theatre and arts centre checked in Gwynedd, Conwy, Denbighshire, Flintshire, Wrexham, Anglesey, Powys, Ceredigion, Pembrokeshire, Carmarthenshire, RCT, Caerphilly, Torfaen, Blaenau Gwent, Merthyr, Bridgend, Monmouthshire, Neath Port Talbot and the Vale of Glamorgan sits in the 250-800 seat band. This is not a claim of completeness: the county-showground population and outdoor/greenfield concert sites remain only partially evidenced (three of the four showgrounds here carry no proven capacity number), and no systematic sweep of hotel ballrooms or university lecture-theatre complexes was performed beyond the largest candidates named above.

venues.scale_description: PROVEN CLOSURE, STATUS NOW ESTABLISHED. The national concert hall of Wales, on The Hayes in central Cardiff, inaugurated 30 August 1982 with its first concert on 11 September 1982. Closed since September 2023 after reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete (RAAC) was found in its roof; a significant number of the 900-plus roof panels are rated 'red - critical' or 'red - high risk'. Because the building is listed, listed-building consent is required before works can start, and repairs are estimated at around GBP 50m and up to 18 months once consent is obtained; reopening is not expected before 2026. Academy Music Group signed a conditional 45-year lease in April 2024 to take over its operation and is preparing the listed-building consent application. This record replaces the census's previous STATUS_REVIEW_REQUIRED with an evidenced CLOSED. The capacity figure is retained at LOW confidence: it comes only from a GRADE_C infobox, and the venue's own site could not be checked because it is closed and cardiff.gov.uk returned 403 in this pass.
venues.no_public_calendar_reason: Venue has been closed since September 2023 pending RAAC roof replacement; no forward programme is published. cardiff.gov.uk's own closure notice page returned HTTP 403 to a plain fetch in this pass.

evidence.note: Seating capacity 1,500; address The Hayes, Cardiff, CF10 1AH; inaugurated 30 August 1982, first concert 11 September 1982; closed since September 2023 due to RAAC in the roof; reopening not expected until 2026 as listed-building consent is required; refurbishment estimated at about GBP 50m; operator Academy Music Group under a conditional 45-year lease.

Cardiff Council's own closure notice was attempted as the GRADE_A source for the closure but returned HTTP 403 Forbidden. Logged so the gap in first-party evidence is explicit rather than papered over.

venues.scale_description: Under construction. A 16,500-capacity indoor arena at Atlantic Wharf, Cardiff Bay, part of an approximately 30-acre mixed-use regeneration consented in early 2023, owned by Cardiff Council and to be operated by Live Nation UK; architects Populous and HOK, main contractor McLaren.
